primitives.name: An alpha-approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and, on every instance, returns a solution within a factor alpha of optimal (alpha > 1 for minimization, alpha < 1 for maximization); alpha is its performance guarantee (Definition 1.1).
primitives.verbatim_quote: for all instances of the problem produces a solution whose value is within a factor of α of the value of an optimal solution.
assumptions: The problem has an objective function mapping each solution to a nonnegative value.
Polynomial time is measured in the input size.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Worst-case over all instances: the guarantee can be far looser than typical performance, and for some problems (maximum clique) no nontrivial alpha exists unless P = NP.

layer2.mapping: The engine treats every heuristic signal as an approximation algorithm: it must carry an explicit worst-case factor against the best achievable value, not a vibe. A signal with no stated factor is an unanalyzed heuristic and is labeled as such.
layer2.telemetry: Per-signal backtests: realized value versus best-known value on the same instance set, so the empirical factor can be compared with the claimed one.

primitives.name: A polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) is a family of algorithms A_epsilon, one for each epsilon > 0, achieving factor (1+epsilon) for minimization or (1-epsilon) for maximization; knapsack and Euclidean TSP have one (Definition 1.2).
primitives.verbatim_quote: Many problems have polynomial-time approximation schemes. In later chapters we will encounter the knapsack problem and the Euclidean traveling salesman problem, each of which has a PTAS.
assumptions: Epsilon > 0 is given as part of the family parameter.
Running time may depend arbitrarily on 1/epsilon for a PTAS.
primitives.breakdown_regime: A PTAS need not be practical: the dependence on 1/epsilon can be exponential, which is why the stricter FPTAS notion exists.

layer2.mapping: A tunable accuracy knob with a proven price: the engine can offer the same dial, spending more compute for a provably smaller error factor, and must state the compute cost of each dial setting.
layer2.telemetry: Compute time per accuracy setting measured on fixed instance suites.

primitives.name: Replace integrality in an integer program by nonnegativity to get an LP relaxation solvable in polynomial time; its optimum bounds the true optimum (Z_LP <= OPT for minimization), and the bound is the yardstick every rounding is charged against.
primitives.verbatim_quote: Using a polynomial-time solvable relaxation of a problem in order to obtain a lower bound (in the case of minimization problems) or an upper bound (in the case of maximization problems) on the optimum value of the problem is a concept that will appear frequently in this book.
primitives.latex: \min \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j x_j \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{j:\, e_i \in S_j} x_j \ge 1, \; i=1,\dots,n, \quad x_j \in \{0,1\}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.w_j: weight (cost) of subset S_j, nonnegative, cost units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_j: indicator decision variable: 1 if subset S_j is selected, 0 otherwise, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.e_i: element i of the ground set E that must be covered
symbol_and_unit_ledger.S_j: subset j of the ground set

assumptions: Every integer-feasible solution is feasible for the relaxation with the same objective value.
Linear programs are solvable in polynomial time.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The relaxation can be weak: its optimum may sit far below OPT, and then no rounding charged against it can certify a good factor (see the integrality gap).

layer2.mapping: Relax the engine's discrete choices (which signals fire, which games qualify) into continuous weights, solve the easy continuous problem, and use its value as a certified bound on the best any discrete policy could do before rounding back.
layer2.telemetry: Continuous weight solutions per decision cycle plus the bound gap between relaxed and rounded objective values.

primitives.page: Section 1.2, book pp. 17-18 (programs (1.1) and (1.2)); text line 625

primitives.name: Threshold rounding of the set cover LP: include set S_j iff x_j >= 1/f, where f is the maximum number of sets containing any element; this is an f-approximation, and for vertex cover (f = 2) a 2-approximation (Theorem 1.6).
primitives.verbatim_quote: In the special case of the vertex cover problem, fi = 2 for each vertex i ∈ V , since each edge is incident to exactly two vertices. Thus, the rounding algorithm gives a 2-approximation algorithm for the vertex cover problem.
assumptions: f is the maximum frequency of any element across the sets.
An optimal LP solution is available.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The factor degrades linearly in f; for general set cover f can be as large as m, making the guarantee useless, and the per-instance ratio against Z_LP (the a fortiori guarantee) is the informative number.

layer2.mapping: Convert continuous confidence weights into discrete include/exclude decisions with a threshold set by the maximum overlap of any item; the proof pattern (each constraint forces one large coordinate) certifies the cost of the discretization in advance.
layer2.telemetry: Weight distributions per item, overlap counts (max number of lists any item appears on), realized cost of the rounded set versus the LP bound.

primitives.name: Weak duality: every feasible dual solution has value no greater than every feasible primal solution, so any dual feasible solution is a certificate bounding OPT from below (for minimization).
primitives.verbatim_quote: any feasible solution to the dual linear program has a value no greater than any feasible solution to the primal linear program
assumptions: Both primal and dual are linear programs in standard form.
The dual has one variable per primal constraint and one constraint per primal variable.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Weak duality alone gives no tightness: the dual bound can be strictly below the primal optimum for integer programs, and it says nothing about how to construct a good dual solution.

layer2.mapping: Every claim the engine makes should ship with a dual-style certificate: an independently checkable lower bound (an opposing priced argument) that the claimed solution cannot beat, so quality is audited against an adversary's bound, not against itself.
layer2.telemetry: Certificate values logged beside each decision: claimed objective versus the best opposing bound found.

primitives.name: Strong duality: if both primal and dual LPs are feasible, their optimal values are exactly equal; the dual optimum is not just a bound but the exact price of the primal problem.
primitives.verbatim_quote: Strong duality states that as long as there exist feasible solutions to both the primal and dual linear programs, their optimal values are equal.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_j^{*}: optimal primal LP variable for set j, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.y_i^{*}: optimal dual price charged to element i, cost units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w_j: weight of set S_j, cost units

assumptions: Feasible solutions exist for both the primal and the dual LP.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Applies to linear programs only: once integrality is imposed, a duality gap generally opens, and the gap is exactly the integrality gap that caps LP-based guarantees.

layer2.mapping: When the engine prices a resource two ways (direct cost versus shadow prices of the constraints it consumes) and the two disagree, the disagreement itself is a measurable defect to investigate, because in the relaxed problem they must coincide.
layer2.telemetry: Paired valuations per decision: direct objective value and shadow-price valuation, with the gap tracked over time.

primitives.name: Complementary slackness: at optimality, a nonzero primal (or dual) variable forces the corresponding dual (or primal) constraint to be tight; this characterizes optimal solutions and tells a rounding which sets the dual has fully paid for.
primitives.verbatim_quote: whenever a linear programming variable (primal or dual) is nonzero, the corresponding constraint in the dual or primal is tight. These conditions are known as the complementary slackness conditions.
assumptions: Both solutions are feasible for their respective programs.
Equality of primal and dual objective values (strong duality) holds.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exact complementary slackness holds only at exact optima; approximate solutions satisfy it only approximately, so algorithms use relaxed versions and pay for the slack in the factor.

layer2.mapping: An attribution rule for the engine: a factor may be credited with driving a decision only if its constraint is tight, meaning the factor is actually binding at the margin; slack factors get zero credit even if correlated with the outcome.
layer2.telemetry: Per-decision binding tests: which input constraints are tight at the chosen solution and which carry slack.

primitives.name: Dual rounding: take an optimal dual solution and select every set whose dual constraint is tight; the selected sets form a cover costing at most f times optimal, because each element's price is charged at most f times (Theorem 1.8).
primitives.verbatim_quote: The dual rounding algorithm described above is an f -approximation algorithm for the set cover problem.
assumptions: An optimal dual solution is available.
f is the maximum element frequency.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Same f ceiling as primal threshold rounding, and in fact its output is a superset of the primal rounding's output, so it can never beat it on this problem.

layer2.mapping: Select components by whether the opposing priced argument has fully paid for them: an item enters the portfolio of active signals when the sum of prices assigned to the needs it covers reaches its cost, not when its own score crosses an arbitrary line.
layer2.telemetry: Price accumulations per candidate item versus its activation cost.

primitives.name: The primal-dual method: start from a dual feasible solution, raise dual variables of uncovered elements until a dual constraint goes tight, add that set, and repeat; the primal is built only from tight constraints, giving an f-approximation without solving any LP (Algorithm 1.1, Theorem 1.9).
primitives.verbatim_quote: Primal-dual algorithms start with a dual feasible solution, and use dual information to infer a primal, possibly infeasible, solution. If the primal solution is indeed infeasible, the dual solution is modified to increase the value of the dual objective function.
assumptions: Dual variables start feasible (for example all zero, given nonnegative weights).
Each raise keeps all dual constraints feasible.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The basic schema gives factor f here; better factors need cleanup phases or relaxed complementary slackness, and choosing which dual variables to raise is problem-specific craft, not a generic recipe.

layer2.mapping: A constructive loop the engine can run without a solver: keep raising the internal price of whatever need is currently unmet until some candidate exactly pays for itself, then commit it; prices, not scores, sequence the commitments.
layer2.telemetry: The sequence of price raises and tightness events per decision cycle, plus final price totals as the audit bound.

primitives.page: Section 1.5, book pp. 23-24 (Algorithm 1.1, Theorem 1.9); text line 977

primitives.name: Greedy set cover: repeatedly pick the set minimizing weight per newly covered element; the kth covered element is charged at most OPT/(n-k+1), summing to an H_n (about ln n) approximation (Theorem 1.11).
primitives.verbatim_quote: In each round, we choose the set that gives us the most bang for the buck; that is, the set that minimizes the ratio of its weight to the number of currently uncovered elements it contains.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: number of elements in the ground set

assumptions: Sets are chosen one at a time and never removed.
An optimal solution covers all remaining elements at total weight OPT, so some set always offers average cost at most OPT over the remaining count.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The harmonic factor is essentially best possible for this problem class (see the hardness primitive), and greedy's myopia is real: early cheap-per-element picks can force expensive leftovers on adversarial instances.

layer2.mapping: Marginal-value ranking with a proven decay: when the engine greedily adds signals by value per unit of new coverage, the harmonic analysis prices the myopia in advance, and the per-step charge (OPT divided by what remains uncovered) is a usable stopping statistic.
layer2.telemetry: Marginal coverage per added signal and the remaining uncovered mass after each addition.

primitives.name: Dual fitting: analyze a greedy algorithm by constructing an infeasible dual solution whose value equals the algorithm's cost, then scaling it by one factor (here H_g) to restore feasibility; the scaling factor is the approximation guarantee (Theorem 1.12).
primitives.verbatim_quote: The name dual fitting has been given to this technique of constructing an infeasible dual solution whose value is equal to the value of the primal solution constructed, and such that scaling the dual solution by a single value makes it feasible.
assumptions: The constructed dual charges each element exactly once, when it is first covered.
g is the maximum set size, bounding the harmonic sum that must be scaled away.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The fitted dual is not the optimal dual, so the bound can be loose; the method certifies a factor but does not improve the algorithm, and it needs a charging scheme tailored to the algorithm's choices.

layer2.mapping: An audit pattern for any engine heuristic: reconstruct the implicit prices its choices imply, check how badly those prices violate the constraints, and report the single scale factor that would make them legal as the heuristic's honest quality grade.
layer2.telemetry: Implied per-item prices from logged decisions and their worst constraint violation ratio.

primitives.name: Hardness wall for set cover: some constant c > 0 exists such that a c ln n approximation for unweighted set cover would imply P = NP, so the greedy harmonic guarantee is optimal up to constants (Theorem 1.14).
primitives.verbatim_quote: There exists some constant c > 0 such that if there exists a c ln n-approximation algorithm for the unweighted set cover problem, then P = NP.
assumptions: The statement is conditional on P not equal NP.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The wall is asymptotic and worst-case: structured real instances may admit much better factors, and the constant c from the proof is not the operative limit in practice.

layer2.mapping: A stop rule for tuning effort: once a component's guarantee reaches a proven hardness wall for its problem class, further optimization of that component is wasted motion and the engine should reallocate effort to instance structure instead.
layer2.telemetry: Problem-class tags per engine component with the known hardness constant for the class.

primitives.name: Randomized rounding with repetition: include each set independently with probability x_j, repeated c ln n times (include if any trial succeeds); the expected cost is O(ln n) times the LP value and every element is covered with high probability (Theorem 1.17).
primitives.verbatim_quote: The algorithm is a randomized O(ln n)-approximation algorithm that produces a set cover with high probability.
primitives.latex: \Pr[e_i \text{ not covered}] = \prod_{j:\, e_i \in S_j} (1 - x_j^{*}) \le e^{-\sum_{j:\, e_i \in S_j} x_j^{*}} \le e^{-1}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_j^{*}: optimal fractional LP value for set j, in [0,1], dimensionless probability
symbol_and_unit_ledger.e_i: element i that must be covered

assumptions: Rounding events for different sets are independent.
The LP constraint for each element sums the covering x_j to at least 1.
The inequality 1 - x <= e^{-x} holds for all x.
primitives.breakdown_regime: One round leaves each element uncovered with probability up to e^{-1}; only repetition plus a union bound gives high probability, at the price of the ln n factor in expected cost, and the expectation is conditional on feasibility in the analysis.

layer2.mapping: Fractional confidences can be sampled rather than thresholded: interpret each weight as an inclusion probability, repeat the sampling logarithmically many times, and the union bound prices the residual miss probability explicitly instead of hiding it.
layer2.telemetry: Realized miss rates per item across repeated samples versus the e^{-1} per-round bound.

primitives.name: Uniform random assignment for MAX SAT: setting each variable true independently with probability 1/2 satisfies each clause with probability 1 - (1/2)^{l_j} >= 1/2, a randomized 1/2-approximation by linearity of expectation (Theorem 5.1).
primitives.verbatim_quote: A very straightforward use of randomization for MAX SAT is to set each xi to true independently with probability 1/2.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.l_j: number of literals in clause C_j, count

assumptions: Variables are set independently.
Every clause has at least one literal.
Clause weights are nonnegative.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The 1/2 comes from unit clauses; long clauses do much better, so the guarantee understates performance on clause-length-rich instances, and the guarantee is in expectation, not per run.

layer2.mapping: A null-model floor for the engine: a coin-flip policy already banks half of the achievable weighted score on satisfiability-style objectives, so any learned policy must be graded against the random baseline's expectation, not against zero.
layer2.telemetry: Objective value of the uniform random policy estimated by simulation on each instance family.

primitives.name: MAX E3SAT (exactly 3 literals per clause): the random algorithm's 7/8 guarantee is exactly optimal; any (7/8 + epsilon) approximation for any constant epsilon > 0 implies P = NP (Theorem 5.2).
primitives.verbatim_quote: Consider the case in which lj = 3 for all clauses j; this restriction of the problem is sometimes called MAX E3SAT, since there are exactly 3 literals in each clause.
assumptions: Each clause has exactly 3 literals.
The hardness is conditional on P not equal NP and comes from probabilistically checkable proofs.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The wall is specific to worst-case 3-literal instances; it does not preclude better factors on instances with longer clauses or exploitable structure.

layer2.mapping: Some of the engine's sub-objectives have a provable ceiling set by their clause structure: when the ceiling is reached by the trivial algorithm, sophistication adds nothing and the correct move is to change the instance representation, not the solver.
layer2.telemetry: Distribution of constraint lengths in the engine's objective encodings, flagged where the trivial algorithm is already optimal.

primitives.name: Random partition for MAX CUT: placing each vertex in U independently with probability 1/2 puts each edge in the cut with probability 1/2, giving expected cut weight at least half of optimal (Theorem 5.3).
primitives.verbatim_quote: Here we place each vertex v ∈ V into U independently with probability 1/2.
primitives.latex: E[Z] = \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} \Pr[(i,j) \text{ in cut}] = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} \ge \tfrac{1}{2} OPT

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Z: total weight of edges crossing the cut, weight units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.U: one side of the random partition of V

assumptions: Vertex placements are independent.
Edge weights are nonnegative, so total edge weight upper-bounds OPT.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Half is weak when the graph has strong community structure the random split ignores; it is a floor to beat (Goemans-Williamson reaches 0.878), not a target.

layer2.mapping: For partition-style decisions (splitting items into two camps), independent coin flips define the provable floor of half the total crossing weight; the engine's structured splitter must report its margin over exactly this floor.
layer2.telemetry: Crossing weight of the random policy versus the structured policy on the same graphs.

primitives.name: Derandomization by conditional expectations: fix variables one at a time, each time choosing the value that maximizes the conditional expectation of the objective given previous choices; the invariant that the conditional expectation never drops yields a deterministic algorithm with the randomized guarantee.
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is sometimes called the method of conditional expectations, due to its use of conditional expectations.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.W: total weight of satisfied clauses, weight units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.E[W | x_1 <- b]: expected objective given x_1 set to b and the rest still random

assumptions: Variables are set independently in the randomized algorithm.
Each conditional expectation is computable in polynomial time.
The maximum of the two conditional expectations is at least their average.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when conditional expectations cannot be computed or approximated efficiently (for example with complex dependencies between variables), and the greedy one-variable-at-a-time fixing cannot revisit earlier choices.

layer2.mapping: The engine can make randomized policies deterministic without losing their proven value: commit choices sequentially, each time keeping the branch whose expected outcome is higher, which converts an in-expectation guarantee into a guaranteed realized outcome.
layer2.telemetry: Conditional expected objective before and after each committed choice, verifying the never-decreasing invariant.

primitives.name: Biasing the coin beats 1/2 for MAX SAT: setting each variable true with probability p = (sqrt(5)-1)/2 (about 0.618) guarantees min(p, 1-p^2) = p in expectation, a randomized 0.618-approximation, by balancing unit clauses against longer clauses (Lemma 5.4, Theorems 5.5 and 5.7).
primitives.verbatim_quote: If each xi is set to true with probability p > 1/2 independently, then the probability that any given clause is satisfied is at least min(p, 1−p2 ) for MAX SAT instances with no negated unit clauses.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.p: probability of setting a variable true, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.1 - p^2: lower bound on satisfaction probability for clauses of length at least 2

assumptions: Initial analysis assumes no negated unit clauses; the extension reweights the OPT bound by unit-clause weights (Lemma 5.6).
Variables are set independently with the same p.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The optimum p balances only two clause classes; richer clause-length distributions admit better tuned or per-variable biases, and the guarantee is again in expectation.

layer2.mapping: A single global bias knob, set by equating the worst-case returns of two regimes, buys a provable improvement over the symmetric default: the engine should tune its global thresholds by exactly this minimax balancing, not by grid search folklore.
layer2.telemetry: Regime-conditional success rates as a function of the global bias parameter, locating the crossing point empirically.

primitives.name: Integrality gap (Definition 5.13): the worst-case ratio of integer optimum to LP optimum over all instances; if a formulation has gap rho, no algorithm whose guarantee is proven relative to that LP can beat rho. The MAX SAT formulation's gap is exactly 3/4, matching its best LP-based guarantee.
primitives.verbatim_quote: The integrality gap of an integer program is the worst-case ratio over all instances of the problem of value of an optimal solution to the integer programming formulation to value of an optimal solution to its linear programming relaxation.
assumptions: The ratio is taken over all instances of the problem.
For maximization the ratio is integer value over LP value, at most 1.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The gap is a property of the formulation, not the problem: a stronger formulation (more constraints) can shrink it, and algorithms not charged against the LP (for example SDP-based ones) are not bound by it.

layer2.mapping: Before trusting any engine bound, measure the gap of the relaxation it rests on: the worst observed ratio between the true discrete optimum and the relaxed optimum caps every certificate the relaxation can issue, and a bad instance exhibiting the gap should be kept as a permanent regression test.
layer2.telemetry: Instance library of worst observed relaxed-versus-true ratios per problem family.

primitives.name: Chernoff bounds (Theorem 5.23): for a sum X of independent 0-1 variables with mean mu bracketed by L <= mu <= U, the tail probabilities Pr[X >= (1+delta)U] and Pr[X <= (1-delta)L] decay exponentially, via Markov's inequality applied to e^{tX}; this is what turns randomized rounding expectations into high-probability guarantees.
primitives.verbatim_quote: In essence, the theorems say that it is very likely that the sum of n independent 0-1 random variables is not far away from the expected value of the sum.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.L, U: lower and upper bounds on mu

assumptions: The variables are independent (identically distributed is not required).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Independence is essential: correlated rounding breaks the bound, which is why analyses using it must verify or enforce limited dependence; the bounds are also loose for very small means.

layer2.mapping: Concentration is the engine's license to trust aggregate signals: when many near-independent weak indicators are summed, Chernoff tails bound how far the total can sit from its mean, and the bound degrades exactly when the indicators correlate, which is measurable.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical tail frequencies of summed signals versus the Chernoff prediction, plus pairwise correlation audits of the summands.

primitives.name: Semidefinite programming: a linear objective and linear constraints plus a matrix variable constrained to be positive semidefinite (X psd iff y^T X y >= 0 for all y); SDPs are solvable in polynomial time to within additive epsilon (Definition 6.1 and program (6.1)).
primitives.verbatim_quote: A semidefinite program (SDP) is similar to a linear program in that there is a linear objective function and linear constraints. In addition, however, a square symmetric matrix of variables can be constrained to be positive semidefinite.
primitives.latex: \max \; \sum_{i,j} c_{ij} x_{ij} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i,j} a_{ijk} x_{ij} = b_k \; \forall k, \quad X = (x_{ij}) \succeq 0

symbol_and_unit_ledger.X psd, X >= 0 in the psd order: all eigenvalues nonnegative; y^T X y >= 0 for all y

assumptions: X is symmetric.
Standard technical conditions (described in the chapter notes) hold for polynomial-time solvability to additive error epsilon.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Solutions carry an additive error epsilon and running time polynomial in log(1/epsilon); exact optima are not obtained, and very large SDPs are far slower in practice than LPs.

layer2.mapping: Lift pairwise relationships into a Gram matrix and demand global consistency (positive semidefiniteness): the engine can relax binary agreement variables into vectors whose inner products must form a valid Gram matrix, a strictly stronger relaxation than pairwise LP constraints.
layer2.telemetry: Eigenvalue spectra of the engine's pairwise-agreement matrices; negative eigenvalues measure global inconsistency.

primitives.name: SDP equals vector program: a symmetric matrix X is psd iff X = V^T V, so SDP variables can be read as vectors v_i with x_{ij} = v_i . v_j; this is what makes geometric rounding of SDP solutions possible.
primitives.verbatim_quote: We claim that in fact the SDP (6.1) and the vector program (6.2) are equivalent. This follows from Fact 6.2; in particular, it follows since a symmetric X is psd if and only if X = V T V for some matrix V .
primitives.latex: X = V^{T} V, \qquad x_{ij} = v_i \cdot v_j

symbol_and_unit_ledger.V: matrix whose columns are the vectors v_i
symbol_and_unit_ledger.v_i: vector assigned to variable i, in R^n
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_{ij}: inner product of v_i and v_j

assumptions: X is symmetric.
A factorization V with X = V^T V can be computed in polynomial time (to within small error).
primitives.breakdown_regime: The dimension of the vectors can be as large as n, so the geometric picture is high-dimensional; intuition from 2D or 3D (angles, hemispheres) must be re-proven, usually via the Gaussian facts of Section 6.2.

layer2.mapping: Every pairwise score the engine keeps should be factorizable: if predicted pairwise affinities cannot be realized as inner products of unit vectors, the affinity table is internally inconsistent and any downstream rounding inherits that inconsistency.
layer2.telemetry: Factorization residual when approximating the engine's affinity matrices by Gram matrices of bounded dimension.

primitives.name: MAX CUT vector relaxation: replace each yi in {+1,-1} by a unit vector v_i and y_i y_j by v_i . v_j, maximizing (1/2) sum w_ij (1 - v_i . v_j); the relaxation value upper-bounds OPT and feeds the hyperplane rounding (program (6.4)).
primitives.verbatim_quote: We will now use semidefinite programming to give a .878-approximation algorithm for the problem in general graphs.
primitives.latex: \max \; \frac{1}{2} \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} \big(1 - v_i \cdot v_j\big) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad v_i \cdot v_i = 1, \; v_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.v_i . v_j: inner product; equals y_i y_j when vectors collapse to the line

assumptions: Any feasible sign assignment embeds as vectors on a line with the same value, so the relaxation value is at least OPT.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The relaxation can overvalue instances whose optimal vectors spread in high dimensions; its integrality gap is exactly the 0.878 constant, so no rounding of this relaxation beats it in the worst case.

layer2.mapping: Embed the two camps of a partition problem as directions on a sphere: items that should separate get near-opposite vectors, and the relaxed objective prices the embedding before any hard assignment is made.
layer2.telemetry: The SDP objective value per instance as an upper bound certificate beside the realized cut weight.

primitives.name: Random hyperplane rounding: draw a Gaussian vector r and put vertex i on the side its vector v_i points (sign of v_i . r); edge (i,j) is cut with probability (1/pi) arccos(v_i . v_j), converting angles into cut probabilities (Lemma 6.7).
primitives.verbatim_quote: Another way of looking at this algorithm is that we consider the hyperplane with normal r containing the origin.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.r: random vector with independent N(0,1) components
symbol_and_unit_ledger.v_i, v_j: unit vectors from the SDP solution
symbol_and_unit_ledger.arccos(v_i . v_j): angle between the two vectors, radians

assumptions: r/||r|| is uniform on the unit sphere (Fact 6.4).
All v_i have unit length.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The probability depends only on the pairwise angle, so global structure beyond angles is discarded; highly clustered vector configurations can make many edges share fate through the same hyperplane.

layer2.mapping: Turn soft directional embeddings into hard two-way decisions by a random linear probe: the separation probability of two items is an exact function of their angle, so the engine can price disagreements before committing to a split.
layer2.telemetry: Realized separation rates per pair bucketed by embedding angle, checked against the arccos law.

primitives.name: The Goemans-Williamson analysis: since (1/pi) arccos(x) >= 0.878 * (1/2)(1 - x) for all x in [-1,1] (Lemma 6.8), random hyperplane rounding of the MAX CUT SDP is a 0.878-approximation, and the constant is the integrality gap of the relaxation (Theorem 6.9).
primitives.verbatim_quote: We now begin the proof that choosing a random hyperplane gives a .878-approximation algorithm for the problem.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x: inner product v_i . v_j of two unit vectors, in [-1,1]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.0.878: minimum over x of the ratio of the two sides, dimensionless

assumptions: The inequality is verified by calculus over the whole interval [-1,1].
Expectation is over the random hyperplane only.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The constant is tight for this relaxation: instances meeting it with equality exist, and beating 0.878 for MAX CUT in general requires a different relaxation or (under the unique games conjecture) is impossible.

layer2.mapping: A termwise domination audit: the GW proof works because the rounding's success probability dominates the relaxed contribution edge by edge with one universal constant; the engine should demand the same per-term domination, with the worst term setting the advertised factor.
layer2.telemetry: Per-pair ratio of realized separation probability to relaxed contribution; the minimum ratio is the certified factor.

primitives.page: Section 6.2, book p. 144 (proof lead-in to Theorem 6.9); text lines 7649-7650

primitives.name: Ellipsoid method plus separation oracle: an LP with exponentially many constraints is solvable in time polynomial in the number of variables and the encoding length, given a polynomial-time oracle that either certifies feasibility or returns a violated constraint; running time does not depend on the number of constraints.
primitives.verbatim_quote: In the notes at the end of the chapter, we sketch how a polynomial-time separation oracle leads to a polynomial-time algorithm for solving LPs with exponentially many constraints.
assumptions: A bound phi on the bits needed to encode any single constraint is given.
The separation oracle runs in polynomial time.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The ellipsoid method is a polynomiality proof, not a practical solver; the book itself recommends the heuristic loop of solving over a small constraint subset and adding violated constraints as found.

layer2.mapping: Do not enumerate the engine's constraint set: keep a checker that, given a candidate decision, returns the single most violated requirement, and iterate; feasibility is maintained by an oracle loop rather than by listing every rule in advance.
layer2.telemetry: Oracle call counts and violated-constraint histories per decision; a rising violation count localizes which requirement family is misspecified.

primitives.name: Farthest-point greedy for k-center: pick an arbitrary first center, then repeatedly add the point farthest from the current centers; the radius achieved is at most twice optimal, by the triangle inequality and a pigeonhole argument on the optimal clusters (Algorithm 2.1, Theorem 2.3).
primitives.verbatim_quote: Algorithm 2.1 is a 2-approximation algorithm for the k-center problem.
primitives.latex: d(i, S) = \min_{j \in S} d_{ij}, \qquad r(S) = \max_{i \in V} d(i, S)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.d_{ij}: distance between vertices i and j, satisfying the triangle inequality, distance units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.r(S): covering radius of S, distance units

assumptions: Distances are symmetric, zero on the diagonal, and obey the triangle inequality.
Exactly k centers must be chosen.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The factor 2 is tight for this algorithm, and the objective is the worst-case radius: one outlier point dictates the radius, so the method is fragile to outliers and to non-metric distances.

layer2.mapping: Worst-point-driven covering: when the engine must place a fixed number of prototypes so no case is far from a prototype, always extend coverage at the currently worst-served case; the factor-2 proof is the template for bounding any such worst-case placement.
layer2.telemetry: Distance of the worst-served case after each center addition, and the full coverage-radius curve.

primitives.page: Section 2.2, book pp. 37-39 (Algorithm 2.1, Theorem 2.3); text line 1812

primitives.name: Scaling plus dynamic programming gives an FPTAS for knapsack: round each value down to a multiple of mu = epsilon M / n (M the largest item value), solve the rounded instance exactly by DP; total value loss is at most n mu = epsilon M <= epsilon OPT, in time O(n^3/epsilon) (Definition 3.4, Theorem 3.5).
primitives.verbatim_quote: A fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPAS, FPTAS) is an approximation scheme such that the running time of Aϵ is bounded by a polynomial in 1/ϵ.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu: rounding unit for values, value units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.M: maximum item value, a lower bound on OPT
symbol_and_unit_ledger.v_i': rounded (scaled) value of item i, integer

assumptions: Item values are nonnegative integers (or measured in integer multiples).
A single most valuable item fits, so M <= OPT.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The scheme exists because knapsack's DP is only pseudo-polynomial; strongly NP-hard problems admit no FPTAS unless P = NP, and the rounding error argument needs the M <= OPT anchor.

layer2.mapping: Controlled precision loss as a compute strategy: quantize the engine's value estimates at a granularity derived from the error budget and the largest single value, solve the coarse problem exactly, and carry the quantization bound as part of the result.
layer2.telemetry: Chosen granularity mu per run with its implied worst-case value loss n*mu logged beside the solution.

primitives.page: Section 3.1, book pp. 67-68 (Definition 3.4, Algorithm 3.2, Theorem 3.5); text line 3246

primitives.name: Lagrangean relaxation: delete a complicating constraint (here the cardinality bound sum y_i <= k for k-median) and add a penalty lambda per unit of violation to the objective, turning the problem into an easier one (here uncapacitated facility location) whose solutions can be traded off by varying lambda (Section 7.7).
primitives.verbatim_quote: In Lagrangean relaxation, we eliminate complicating constraints but add penalties for their violation to the objective function.
primitives.latex: \min \; \sum_{i \in F, j \in D} c_{ij} x_{ij} + \lambda \sum_{i \in F} y_i - \lambda k

symbol_and_unit_ledger.lambda: penalty price per opened facility beyond the budget, cost units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.c_{ij}: assignment cost of client j to facility i, cost units

assumptions: lambda >= 0.
The relaxed problem (without the cardinality constraint) is solvable or approximable.
primitives.breakdown_regime: No single lambda need produce a solution meeting the constraint exactly; algorithms binary-search lambda and combine nearby solutions, and the Lagrangean bound can be strictly weaker than the LP bound.

layer2.mapping: Convert a hard budget on how many signals may fire into a per-use price and sweep the price: the engine gets a family of solutions indexed by lambda, and the right operating point is where the realized count crosses the budget, with the price itself reporting the budget's shadow cost.
layer2.telemetry: Solution count and objective as functions of lambda across the sweep, with the crossing point recorded.

primitives.page: Section 7.7, book pp. 185-186 (programs (7.7) and (7.8)); text line 9998

primitives.name: Probabilistic tree approximation of metrics (Fakcharoenphol-Rao-Talwar): any metric can be randomly embedded into a tree metric that never contracts distances and stretches each pair by O(log n) in expectation, and Omega(log n) is unavoidable in general (Theorem 8.17).
primitives.verbatim_quote: However, we can give a randomized algorithm for producing a tree T such that for each u, v ∈ V , duv ≤ Tuv and E[Tuv ] ≤ O(log n)duv ; that is, the expected distortion is O(log n).
primitives.latex: d_{uv} \le T_{uv}, \qquad E[T_{uv}] \le O(\log n) \, d_{uv}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.d_{uv}: distance in the original metric, distance units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.T_{uv}: distance in the random tree metric, distance units
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: number of points in the metric

assumptions: Pairwise distances are at least 1 for distinct points (a scaling normalization).
The tree may use Steiner nodes beyond V.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Worst-case (deterministic) distortion is linear for some metrics (a cycle needs (n-1)/8), so the guarantee is inherently distributional; a single sampled tree can still stretch a given pair badly.

layer2.mapping: Replace a messy similarity space with a random hierarchy: distances only grow, expected growth is logarithmic, and tree-structured reasoning (dynamic programming over the hierarchy) becomes available at a priced distortion.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical stretch distribution per pair over sampled trees versus the O(log n) expectation.

primitives.name: Iterated rounding: solve the LP, permanently fix every variable that is already large (x_e >= 1/2) in a basic optimal solution, update the residual requirements, re-solve, and repeat; a counting argument on basic solutions guarantees a large variable always exists, giving Jain's 2-approximation for survivable network design (Section 11.3).
primitives.verbatim_quote: Because we iteratively round up the LP solution to create the final feasible solution, this technique is called iterated rounding.
assumptions: The requirement function f is weakly supermodular, which drives the counting argument that some variable in a basic solution is at least 1/2.
Each residual LP is solvable in polynomial time (via a separation oracle).
primitives.breakdown_regime: The method leans entirely on the structure of basic solutions for this constraint family; for general integer programs no such large-variable guarantee exists, and each iteration re-solves an LP, so it is not cheap.

layer2.mapping: Commit in waves: lock the decisions the relaxed solution is most confident about, recompute the residual problem with those commitments priced in, and repeat; the existence proof for a confident decision at each wave is the discipline that keeps the loop from stalling.
layer2.telemetry: Per-wave counts of locked decisions and the maximum fractional value remaining, verifying a >= 1/2 candidate exists each wave.

primitives.name: The unique games conjecture: for any epsilon, delta > 0 there is a label size k such that distinguishing unique games instances with at least a 1-epsilon fraction of satisfiable constraints from instances with at most a delta fraction satisfiable is NP-hard; if true, many SDP-based constants (including 0.878 for MAX CUT and 2 for vertex cover) are exactly optimal.
primitives.verbatim_quote: Given any ϵ, δ > 0, there exists some k > 0 depending on ϵ and δ, such that for the unique games problem with a universe of size k, it is NP-hard to distinguish between instances in which at least a 1 − ϵ fraction of the constraints can be satisﬁed, and instances in which at most a δ fraction of the constraints can be satisﬁed.
assumptions: The conjecture is unproven; results depending on it are conditional.
Checking whether all constraints are satisfiable is polynomial-time by label propagation, so the hardness is purely about near-satisfiability.
primitives.breakdown_regime: It is a conjecture, not a theorem: building on it means the hardness conclusions collapse if it is refuted, and for small label sizes the problem is now known to admit subexponential algorithms, narrowing where the conjecture can bite.

layer2.mapping: A boundary marker for the engine's consistency objectives: past a certain point, telling a nearly consistent labeling from an almost unsatisfiable one is conjectured intractable, so consistency scores should be reported as approximations with stated factors, never as exact satisfiability verdicts.
layer2.telemetry: Label size and constraint satisfaction rates for the engine's consistency checks, with results labeled conditional where the conjecture is invoked.

primitives.name: Sparsest cut via l1 embedding: every n-point metric embeds into l1 with distortion O(log n) (Theorem 15.4), l1 metrics decompose into cut metrics, and minimizing the sparsity over the decomposition's support yields a randomized O(log n)-approximation for sparsest cut (Theorem 15.5).
primitives.verbatim_quote: There is a randomized O(log n)-approximation algorithm for the sparsest cut problem.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho(S): sparsity of cut S: cut cost per unit demand separated, cost per demand unit
symbol_and_unit_ledger.delta(S): set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S

assumptions: The LP relaxation's shortest-path metric dx is well defined from the LP solution.
The l1 embedding is computable in randomized polynomial time with high probability.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The O(log n) distortion is best possible for general metrics, and the approximation inherits that loss; special graph classes (planar, bounded treewidth) admit much better embeddings and hence better factors.

layer2.mapping: To find the weakest separation in a network, embed its distance structure into a space that is literally a mixture of cuts and read the best cut off the mixture: the engine can audit any proposed partition against this relaxation-backed lower bound on sparsity.
layer2.telemetry: Embedding distortion per instance and the sparsity of the best cut found in the decomposition support.

primitives.page: Section 15.1, book pp. 369-370 (Theorems 15.4 and 15.5); text line 20076

primitives.name: Arora-Rao-Vazirani: for the uniform sparsest cut problem (unit demand between every pair), SDP vector solutions with a chaining argument over random projections give an O(sqrt(log n)) performance guarantee, breaking the logarithmic barrier of LP-based methods (Section 15.4).
primitives.verbatim_quote: In this section, we will consider an interesting special case of the problem, the uniform sparsest cut problem. In this case, there is a single unit of demand between each distinct pair of vertices.
assumptions: The SDP solution satisfies the triangle inequalities on the squared distances (an l2^2 metric).
Demands are uniform: one unit between each distinct pair.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The proof is the most involved in the book (the preface singles it out), the guarantee is probabilistic (constant success probability, boosted by repetition), and it applies to the uniform-demand case; general sparsest cut keeps the O(log n) barrier in this treatment.

layer2.mapping: When a partition objective resists LP methods, lift to vectors and argue geometrically: the engine's hardest separation problems should be attacked in the SDP embedding, where separation can be certified against spreading structure rather than single cuts.
layer2.telemetry: Spread statistics of the SDP embedding (how many pairs are far apart) reported with each candidate cut.

primitives.page: Section 15.4, book pp. 385-394 (Algorithm 15.1, Corollary 15.22); text line 20915

primitives.name: Vertex cover is settled modulo the unique games conjecture: the LP rounding factor 2 cannot be improved by any constant amount unless the conjecture fails (Theorem 1.16), and unconditionally no factor below about 1.36 exists unless P = NP (Theorem 1.15).
primitives.verbatim_quote: Assuming the unique games conjecture, if there exists an α-approximation algorithm for the vertex cover problem with constant α < 2, then P = NP.
assumptions: The < 2 statement is conditional on the unique games conjecture.
The unconditional statement rules out factors below 10 sqrt(5) - 21, about 1.36.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Conditional hardness is only as strong as the conjecture; and the statement is about worst-case graphs, so structured graph families (planar, bipartite-like) can and do admit better factors.

layer2.mapping: A worked example of a closed problem for the engine's technique selection: when a simple relaxation's factor is proven optimal (even conditionally), the file on improving that factor is closed and effort moves to exploiting instance structure.
layer2.telemetry: Per-component registry entries marking factors as closed (optimal), open, or formulation-bound.

reasoning_traces.think:
This book is a field manual for a single predicament: most discrete optimization problems worth solving are NP-hard, so the question is not how to solve them but how to solve them with a proof of how much was lost. Its organizing decision, stated in the preface, is to sort the material by design technique rather than by problem: greedy and local search, rounding data with dynamic programming, deterministic rounding of linear programs, randomized rounding of linear and semidefinite programs, the primal-dual method, and cuts and metrics. Each technique is introduced on the set cover problem in Chapter 1 and then revisited across facility location, Steiner problems, scheduling, satisfiability, cuts, and network design, so the reader watches the same problem yield to progressively stronger machinery and learns the techniques as transferable operators rather than as one-off tricks.

The load-bearing object throughout is the linear programming relaxation. An integer program models the problem exactly; relaxing integrality produces a polynomially solvable program whose optimum bounds the true optimum, and every algorithm is then a rounding scheme charged against that bound. Duality is the certification layer: weak duality makes any dual feasible solution a proof of a bound, strong duality makes the bound exact for the relaxation, complementary slackness identifies which primal choices the dual has paid for, and dual fitting turns the whole apparatus into an audit method for algorithms, like greedy, that never touch an LP. The primal-dual method inverts the workflow and builds the dual solution incrementally, raising prices on whatever is still uncovered until a constraint goes tight, which is both an algorithm and a charging argument at once.

Randomization enters as a rounding language: fractional values become probabilities, linearity of expectation does the accounting, Chernoff bounds convert expectations into high-probability statements, and the method of conditional expectations converts the randomized guarantee back into a deterministic one whenever the conditional expectations are computable. The integrality gap is the discipline that keeps all of this honest: it is a property of a formulation, computed from a single bad instance, and it caps every guarantee provable relative to that formulation, as the MAX SAT gap of 3/4 exactly matches its best LP-based algorithm. Semidefinite programming is the escape hatch when the LP gap binds: lifting signs to unit vectors and rounding with a random hyperplane improves MAX CUT from 1/2 to 0.878, with the constant certified termwise by one calculus inequality. The final third of the book is about the geometry of metrics (tree embeddings, l1 embeddings, the Arora-Rao-Vazirani chaining argument) and about the boundary of the whole enterprise: hardness reductions, the PCP theorem, and the unique games conjecture, which together say which approximation factors no algorithm can beat.

For a reasoning engine, the transferable lesson is that a guarantee is a designed artifact, not a byproduct. Every component should be able to state its relaxation (what easier problem its score actually solves), its rounding (how continuous evidence becomes a discrete commitment), and its gap (the worst instance on which its bound is known to be loose). Techniques compose: a Lagrangean relaxation can feed a primal-dual algorithm, whose output can be audited by dual fitting and stress-tested against a gap instance. The book also models intellectual honesty about limits: constants are stated, tight examples are exhibited, conditional results are labeled with the conjecture they depend on, and the ellipsoid method is presented as a polynomiality device while the text openly recommends a different, heuristic loop for actual computation.

Two further threads deserve emphasis. First, the book's treatment of approximation schemes draws a sharp line between problems that admit arbitrarily good guarantees and problems that do not: knapsack yields an FPTAS because its dynamic program is only pseudo-polynomial and value scaling can trade a controlled amount of precision for polynomial running time, while MAX SNP-hard problems admit no PTAS at all unless P equals NP, and the greedy harmonic factor for set cover is already optimal up to constants. This taxonomy matters more than any single algorithm, because it tells the designer where precision is cheap and where it is impossible. Second, the derandomization thread (conditional expectations, pairwise independence, pessimistic estimators in the chapter notes) shows that randomness in these algorithms is usually an accounting device rather than a resource: wherever the expectation argument is explicit, a deterministic algorithm with the same guarantee exists, and the randomized presentation survives because it is simpler to analyze.

The book is equally instructive about what a guarantee does not say. A worst-case factor is a statement about the single most adversarial instance, not about typical performance, and several algorithms here (the simplex-flavored ellipsoid method most starkly) are polynomial in theory and unusable in practice, a distinction the authors flag themselves. Constants proven tight against a relaxation say nothing about stronger formulations: the 3/4 barrier for MAX SAT is a property of one integer program, and the semidefinite lift that follows exists precisely because the barrier was diagnosed as formulation-specific rather than problem-specific. Conditional results carry their own caveat: every theorem resting on the unique games conjecture is a bet, clearly labeled, and the engine that imports such a constant should import the label with it. The net discipline is that each number travels with its scope: the formulation it was charged against, the instance class it quantifies over, and the assumption it depends on.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs from linear programming duality in the 1940s through the greedy analyses for set cover in the 1970s to the probabilistic turn of the late 1980s, when randomized rounding showed that fractional solutions could be sampled rather than thresholded. The 1990s added the primal-dual revival for network design, the Goemans-Williamson semidefinite breakthrough for MAX CUT, and the Fakcharoenphol-Rao-Talwar probabilistic tree embeddings whose illustration is on this book's cover. The 2000s brought the Arora-Rao-Vazirani sublogarithmic sparsest cut result, the PCP-based hardness machinery, and Khot's unique games conjecture as the organizing hypothesis for tight constants. Williamson and Shmoys, writing from the operations research side of the field, consolidate these streams into one design discipline.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The authors model their reader as a graduate student who already believes in proofs and wants transferable technique, not a catalog of problems. Their stated editorial rule is to include only results simple enough to teach in a classroom while remaining central, bending the rule once for Arora-Rao-Vazirani. They believe linear programming is the natural language of approximation even for computer scientists, that a problem is understood when several techniques have been run on it and their guarantees compared, and that worst-case analysis is the only rigorous common currency despite its pessimism, because typical instances cannot be defined honestly. Enthusiasm is explicit: the last reason they give for studying the area is that it is fun.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The hardness layer vetoes optimism elsewhere in the stack. Integrality gaps veto any analysis charged against a weak formulation, regardless of how clever the rounding is. The ln n wall for set cover and the 7/8 wall for MAX E3SAT veto better guarantees for entire problem classes. The unique games conjecture, if true, vetoes improving the SDP constant for MAX CUT or the factor 2 for vertex cover. Complementary slackness vetoes credit assignment: a primal component not backed by a tight dual constraint is uncertified. And the ellipsoid discussion vetoes a naive notion of efficiency: polynomial-time solvability of a relaxation does not imply a usable algorithm, so theoretical feasibility cannot be cited as operational readiness.

universal_lens: Read as a general template, this is a theory of acting well under proven intractability: relax the impossible problem into a tractable one that bounds it, convert the relaxed answer back into a feasible action with a rounding step whose cost is analyzed in advance, and certify the result with a dual argument that an adversary could check. The same three moves (relax, round, certify) describe good practice in forecasting, planning under budgets, and any engineered system that must commit discretely on the basis of continuous evidence while stating, honestly and in advance, how far from optimal the commitment might be.
gsi_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Institute, the book supplies the mathematical spine for teaching bounded rationality as a craft: performance guarantees as the unit of intellectual honesty, duality as the habit of pricing every claim from the opposing side, integrality gaps as the measure of what a simplified model cannot see, and hardness results as the map of where effort stops paying. Its technique-organized structure is also a curriculum design: one problem, many methods, guarantees compared, which is how the Institute teaches any quantitative discipline.
gse_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Edge reasoning engine, the direct imports are operational: score-to-decision conversions should use rounding schemes with stated factors (threshold, randomized with repetition, iterated commitment of the most confident decisions); every published projection should carry a relaxation-based bound it was charged against; greedy signal selection inherits the harmonic analysis and its stopping statistic; budget constraints on how many signals may fire become Lagrangean prices to sweep rather than hard cutoffs; and per-component integrality-gap instances become permanent regression tests that cap what each signal family is allowed to claim.
